source.title: Scrub It Out! Erasing Sensitive Memorization in Code Language Models via Machine Unlearning
source.authors: Zhao-Yang Chu; Yao Wan; Zhi-Kun Zhang; Di Wang; Zhou Yang; Hong-Yu Zhang; Pan Zhou; Xuan-Hua Shi; Hai Jin; David Lo

record.file_problem: None; the full paper is present, though some tables are flattened in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether post-hoc unlearning reduces targeted memorization and preserves coding ability, using code-specific models and memorization measures. It does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The study reports post-unlearning memorization and HumanEval results. Its discussion of extraction attacks and related work is not itself an attack result. The reported EL3, EL5 and EL10 outcomes, HumanEval P@10 outcomes, and other analyses are not included as separate rows under the 60-row limit; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study applies GA, constraint-based (CU) and its own selective CodeEraser unlearning to five code LMs. It reports how well each model still memorizes the targeted sensitive strings verbatim (MA, EL_n), compared against a threshold set by each model's scores on unseen data, and it reports HumanEval utility. That bears on the first two parts of version A (forgetting to a baseline level while keeping general ability) in a new setting: sensitive-string memorization in code models. Section 5.2 says unlearning runs until the thresholds are reached. So falling below the threshold is the stopping rule, and the informative result is how much utility each method keeps at that point. No recovery attack is run, so A's 'simple attacks don't recover it' part and versions B–F are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct but incomplete. The authors conclude that CodeEraser brings targeted sensitive memorization below the unseen-data thresholds efficiently while largely preserving coding utility (e.g. 99.99% retention on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B), and that GA and CU degrade utility more. They acknowledge utility declines at large forget sets (k=256, 512) and high learning rates. They run no recovery attack, though they assert that sub-threshold samples are resistant to extraction attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates gradient-ascent and constraint-based unlearning and introduces a selective, code-sensitive-segment variant; it does not evaluate post-unlearning recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that forgotten-set size, duplication frequency, sensitive-data type, and learning rate affect post-unlearning utility; these analyses are not separately represented in the kept rows.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering
record.problems: The study evaluates five CLM checkpoints from three families and uses five independent runs but reports no error bars or other uncertainty statistics in the extracted tables. It measures memorization against its own unseen-data thresholds, not recovery under the attacks in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row cap, omitted the Table 3 EL3, EL5, and EL10 measures; Table 4 P@10 results; and the separate utility results from Sections 5.4 and 5.5. The kept rows prioritize the primary MA measure and HumanEval P@1/P@5 plus the reported retention aggregate.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks (relearning, prompting, quantization, probing) recover the unlearned sensitive strings; no attack is run. The authors only assert that sub-threshold samples resist extraction.
All: no fine-tuning or relearning attack.
All: no activation ablation or block-vs-delete analysis.
All: no rephrasing, jailbreak or in-context recovery; only a fixed-prefix greedy extraction measure.
CodeEraser is not evaluated against any recovery attack, so robustness is untested.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) Its four row_fixes items named a range ('R01-R15') or comma lists. These are now 60 single-row items. Every row carried the undeclared tag 'V1' and now maps to A, decided from what it measures: forget-set MA (R01–R15) bears on A's forgetting part, and HumanEval P@1/P@5/retention (R16–R60) bears on A's keeping-general-ability part. Row states are unchanged: GA/CU utility is partial, CodeEraser utility is observed except on CodeParrot 1.5B (partial), and all MA rows are observed. Per-row retention percentages were computed from Table 4.
(2) Section 5.2 says unlearning runs until the memorization thresholds are reached. Sub-threshold MA is therefore a stopping rule, not an independent outcome. test_reason and the first label now say so.
(3) The record's stage 'instruct' for the Qwen2.5-Coder-7B rows has no support in the text, which names only Qwen2.5-Coder-7B. This is flagged on those rows.
(4) The five earlier missing entries are dropped: EL3/5/10, P@10, and the Sections 5.4–5.5 utility analyses are all declared in rows_left_out. The text-based limits_scope label is kept and says it rests on text, not rows.
(5) authors_conclusion now adds the authors' own admission of scalability and learning-rate limits.

Other facts: MA measures verbatim recall of secret segments under a fixed prefix with greedy decoding, which is narrower than targeted-knowledge accuracy. The 'near chance' analogue is each model's mean MA on unseen code; for CodeParrot and CodeGen the unseen code is in languages absent from training. No uncertainty is reported, although results average 5 runs. The introduction's 99.00% retention for Qwen conflicts with Table 4's 99.99%. The text contains no instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures targeted memorization reduction and post-unlearning coding performance, but does not test whether simple recovery attacks can or cannot recover the information.
No recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of blocking access versus deleting information is tested.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language change, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
CodeEraser is evaluated for unlearning and utility, not for resistance to the recovery attacks named in the claim.

relationships.condition: Forgetting by GA, CU and CodeEraser on all five code LMs, k=32, MA metric; unlearning runs until the unseen-data thresholds are reached
relationships.reason: Post-unlearning MA falls below the unseen-data threshold in all 15 cells, e.g. Qwen CodeEraser 8.49% vs 40.99% (R01–R15). R09 is marginal (45.13% vs 48.79%). Because the threshold is the stopping rule, this part holds by design.
relationships.display_finding: Memorization accuracy fell below unseen-data thresholds in all 15 settings under a stopping rule requiring those thresholds, including 8.49% versus 40.99% for Qwen CodeEraser and a narrower 45.13% versus 48.79% elsewhere.

relation.reason: Its own forgetting results (MA/EL_n against unseen-data thresholds) and HumanEval results bear on the forgetting and utility parts of version A. It tests no attack part.

tranche.reason: It applies GA, CU and its own CodeEraser to code LMs, a new setting, and reports forgetting and utility results bearing on version A. It uses neither the original's method nor its measure (so not T1). The reader's T2 is defensible but less apt.

source_check.notes: Forgetting is measured as verbatim memorization of sensitive strings (MA, EL_n) against thresholds from unseen data, not accuracy near chance. Unlearning stops at the thresholds, and no recovery attack is run. Qwen's threshold set includes HumanEval, which is also the utility benchmark. The intro gives 99.00% Qwen retention, but Table 4 and Section 5.3 give 99.99%, which matches the table's P@k values. The text never says Qwen2.5-Coder-7B is instruct.

statements.correction: arXiv:2509.13755 (ICSE 2026, reviewed; code released) unlearns memorized sensitive strings in CodeParrot-small 110M, CodeParrot 1.5B, CodeGen-350M/2B-Mono and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with GA, CU and CodeEraser. R01: GA on CodeParrot-small takes MA from 99.74% to 30.71%, below the 45.57% unseen-data threshold. HumanEval retention for CodeEraser is 88.96–102.10%; for GA/CU it is 50.11–89.23%. No attack is run after unlearning.
statements.problem: Cites R01 from this study but gives none of its numbers, so no number is wrong. The CodeLlama leak-rate numbers belong to the separate LLMs4Code study, not this one. The blanket 'Models are 7–70B' is wrong here: this study's models are 110M to 7B. The 'why' line never names this study. The no-attack remark is right: this study runs no relearning, quantization, ablation or extraction attack after unlearning.
